items.prompt: Why does SearchTicketsHandler apply Permissions.CanReadTicket before it applies the caller's Skip and Take?
items.answer: A readable ticket past the first source page would vanish from results
distractors: CanReadTicket runs faster and cheaper once the list is trimmed to a page
The store already checks permissions, so this is only a second pass
Skip and Take throw when the list holds tickets the user cannot read
items.explanation: The guide: if page one holds 100 records the customer cannot read, a matching record on source page two would disappear and the total would describe the wrong population.

items.prompt: The store holds 121 matching tickets and a customer asks for page 1, size 50. How many times does the handler call _store.SearchAsync?
items.answer: Twice at page size 100, since ceil(121 / 100) is 2
distractors: Once, at the caller's own page size of 50 rows
Three times at page size 50, until 121 rows are covered
Twice at page size 50, stopping at the first visible row
items.explanation: The do/while loop requests source pages of 100 until sourcePage passes Math.Max(1, ceil(Total / 100)); 121 rows give 2 source pages, and only then does the handler page the visible list.

items.prompt: A customer searches for a word that appears only in an internal comment on their own ticket. What comes back?
items.answer: Zero results, as only public comments are searched for the term
distractors: Their ticket, since a customer may read every comment on it
Their ticket, with the internal comment removed from the detail
A 403 error, because the query names an internal-only marker
items.explanation: InMemoryTicketStore.SearchAsync only searches comments whose Visibility == CommentVisibility.Public, so an internal note cannot make a customer search match.

items.prompt: An IEnumerable passed to ReplaceTags yields "changed" and then throws. What does the ticket hold afterwards?
items.answer: Its original tags and Version; ToArray threw before Clear ran
distractors: An empty tag list, because _tags.Clear() had already run before the throw
The tags ["changed"], with Version left at its old value
Its original tags, but Version has already advanced by 1
items.explanation: The whole sequence is materialized with ToArray before _tags.Clear(), and Touch runs last; a throw during enumeration leaves tags and version untouched (ReplaceTags_DoesNotPartiallyMutate_WhenEnumerationFails).

items.prompt: ReplaceTags receives {" Billing ", "billing", "VIP"}. What is stored, and how much does Version change?
items.answer: Two tags, billing then vip, and Version rises by exactly 1
distractors: The typed casing Billing and VIP, with Version up by one
Three entries, billing twice plus vip, and Version up by 3
vip first, then billing; Version rises once per tag, so 2
items.explanation: NormalizeTag trims and lowercases, Distinct ignores case, Order sorts; Touch runs once at the end, so Version advances by one.

items.prompt: Two requests both carry expectedVersion 3. The first stores version 4. What happens to the second?
items.answer: It throws ConcurrencyException before its mutation runs
distractors: It overwrites version 4, since the lock lets both writes through
It retries once with version 4, then stores version 5
It waits on _writeLock until the ticket returns to version 3
items.explanation: Under _writeLock the store compares current.Version (4) with expectedVersion (3) and throws before creating the working copy, so mutate is never invoked.

items.prompt: What does SignalRTicketNotifier.TicketUpdatedAsync actually send to clients?
items.answer: Just the name tickets.changed to group inbox, with no payload
distractors: The full TicketSummaryDto, to every connection in the inbox group
The ticket id and new Version, so clients can patch the row
The detail DTO, filtered by CanReadInternalNotes per connection
items.explanation: SendAsync("tickets.changed", cancellationToken) passes no arguments; the ticket parameter only satisfies the interface. Clients refetch through authorized HTTP paths.

items.prompt: Before the fix pass, what happened when Ticket.Create received (TicketPriority)99?
items.answer: The Low due dates from the `_ =>` arms, while reporting priority 99
distractors: It threw an InvalidCastException as soon as the first switch expression ran
It got the Urgent due dates, from the first arm of each switch
It stored no due dates, as both switches returned a null value
items.explanation: A C# enum is an integer underneath, so 99 matched no named arm and fell through to the fallback arm, the Low SLA. Ticket.Create now checks Enum.IsDefined like UpdatePriority.

items.prompt: A customer, on their own ticket, posts a comment with visibility set to Internal. What does CanComment return?
items.answer: false, because the Internal arm needs an Admin, Manager or Agent role
distractors: true, because the customer's user id matches the CustomerEmail
true, and the handler then stores it as a public comment instead
false, because customers cannot comment on any ticket at all
items.explanation: The Internal arm requires a staff role and CanReadTicket; the customer-email clause exists only in the public arm, so changing one JSON enum cannot turn a reply into an internal note.

items.prompt: Why does the SignalR effect in App.tsx use an empty dependency list and read filtersRef/selectedIdRef?
items.answer: Listing [selectedId, filters] made each keystroke reopen the socket
distractors: SignalR forbids more than one handler per event name on a connection
Refs make the inbox list re-render as soon as the filters change
An empty list lets the callback read fresh state out of its closure
items.explanation: The effect cleanup stops the connection, so listing changing values as dependencies tore down the WebSocket on every change. One connection per mount plus refs for the changing values fixes it.

items.prompt: What does TicketSummaryDto deliberately leave out that the detail DTO carries?
items.answer: The ticket description and the comment bodies
distractors: The customer name and the customer email address
The Version number, which only the detail carries
The tag list and the two SLA breach flags
items.explanation: The summary carries number, subject, customer identity, status, priority, assignment, tags, timestamps, breach flags, commentCount and version; description and comments are detail-only.

items.prompt: In the 121-ticket search test, why is the customer's ticket T-000001 on source page 2?
items.answer: The store sorts by UpdatedAt descending, so it is the oldest of 121
distractors: The store sorts by Number ascending, and each page holds 50 rows
LoadSeedTickets inserts it last, after the other 120 tickets
Its internal comment pushes it behind every other ticket that has no notes
items.explanation: The other tickets are created at now.AddSeconds(i), so T-000001 has the oldest UpdatedAt and is row 121 of the descending order, on source page 2.

items.front: Pushing authorization into an EF query: the three rules the guide names?
items.back: Total comes from the same filtered IQueryable as the items; Skip/Take come last (OFFSET/FETCH after WHERE); the projection (.Select) is inside the query, so unselected columns cannot leak.

items.front: What replaces the in-memory expectedVersion check on a relational database?
items.back: A concurrency token (RowVersion or IsConcurrencyToken) so UPDATE ... WHERE Version = @expected hits 0 rows on a stale write and EF raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException (HTTP 409/412); or ExecuteUpdateAsync with a version Where and 0 affected rows meaning someone else got there first.

items.front: React rule for a callback that outlives the render that created it?
items.back: Read changing values from a ref, not from its closure (SignalR/WebSocket handlers, timers, window listeners). Listing them as effect deps recreates the resource too often; [] without a ref acts on mount-time values forever.

items.front: Lesson of the half-applied enum guard in Ticket.Create?
items.back: When you add a guard to a mutator, grep every other entry point that sets the same field; constructors and factory methods are the ones forgotten, and JSON deserialisation can deliver any integer as an enum.
